summary: Bridgewater's Karniol-Tambour argues record US corporate profits depend on spending funded by borrowing, dissaving and fiscal transfers rather than wages. That support is fading as transfers end and labor power rises. Markets price rate rises but not a profit decline, so she is bearish on equities.

coverage.note: profit identity: non-wage spending sources, secular forces
pre-2008 forces, QE, 2020 profit surge via fiscal transfers
turning point: dissaving, rates, labor power, taxes
inflation squeeze, commodity weight, low-return capex, rate duration
what is priced in, 1970s analogy, US exceptionalism

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: for a business to grow its profit margin it has to simply raise revenue or get people to pay for its products without paying labor
claims.claim: Aggregate corporate profit exists only if spending exceeds wage income, so profits are financed by borrowing, dissaving or government deficits rather than by wages.
claims.indicator: US corporate profits relative to GDP
claims.direction: corporate profits up when spending funded by non-wage sources
claims.conditions: for the whole economy, not a single firm
claims.testable: partly - profit share vs credit/deficit/savings flows is measurable

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: most importantly leverage borrowing spending down your savings and so for example households can go and take out a mortgage put on their credit card use their savings
claims.claim: Household borrowing and savings drawdown are channels that let workers buy goods without earning the money, which inflates corporate profits.
claims.direction: profits up when household leverage or dissaving rises
claims.testable: partly - household credit and saving rate series exist

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: businesses can do the same thing when they create capital expenditures because often they go and borrow to do those capital expenditures
claims.claim: Debt-financed corporate capex creates revenue for equipment sellers with no wage payout, so it also supports aggregate profits.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the government can increase the deficit and reduce the deficit
claims.claim: Government deficits supply income that is not paid out as wages, so larger deficits raise corporate profits and smaller deficits cut them.
claims.testable: partly - deficit vs profit share is testable

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: in the decades leading up to the financial crisis basically you had very significant secular forces
claims.claim: Before 2008, secular forces (globalization, deregulation, fewer unions) drove the structural rise in profit share.
claims.testable: no - narrative of structural forces, no sharp signal

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: a lot of deregulation the fact that there are fewer and fewer labor unions you basically had these structural forces that reduced a lot of workers bargaining power
claims.claim: Globalization, deregulation and union decline cut worker bargaining power, so wages lagged and workers borrowed to keep spending, raising profits.
claims.direction: wage share down, profit share up
claims.testable: partly - wage share and union density are measurable

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: saving dollars drove interest rates down and that whole process of lowering the interest rates interest
claims.claim: Emerging-market and oil-producer dollar saving pushed rates down for years, which let private borrowers keep funding spending that supported profits.
claims.indicator: EM and oil exporter reserve accumulation, interest rates

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: a lot of the borrowing that was done whether it's housing and subprime couldn't really be done anymore
claims.claim: After the financial crisis private-sector leveraging ended and the government took over as the source of non-wage spending.
claims.direction: private leverage down, government deficit up

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: lots of money is printed lots of people get that money but really drives up financial assets and wealthy people own financial assets disproportionately
claims.claim: QE mostly lifts financial assets owned by the wealthy, who spend little of the gain, so it supports demand weakly per dollar and raises inequality.
claims.direction: financial assets up, spending boost small
claims.testable: partly - marginal propensity to spend by wealth bucket

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: corporate profits actually surged to new highs now that doesn't usually happen
claims.claim: In 2020 profits rose to record highs while the economy collapsed, an unusual disconnect between profits and activity.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the government gave people a significant amount of money that actually more than offsets all the wages that they lost
claims.claim: Direct fiscal transfers that exceeded lost wages let households keep spending while firms cut payroll, the ideal setup for record profits.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the bottom 60 or 80 of households had the fastest healing and balance sheets we've ever seen
claims.claim: Stimulus checks repaired household balance sheets very fast, which left households able to spend from savings later.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the last couple months not many months but two three months of spending have been totally totally funded by households basically dis saving
claims.claim: With transfers gone, spending is being funded by lower saving rates and credit card borrowing, which cannot be sustained to push profits higher.
claims.indicator: personal saving rate, credit card borrowing
claims.direction: spending growth down once dissaving ends
claims.testable: yes - saving rate and card credit are published

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: rates are rising and we already have the biggest rise in mortgage rates in decades very very fast very very rapid falling asset prices this isn't going to be the time that households choose
claims.claim: Rising rates and falling asset prices make households unlikely to lever up or save less again, so debt cannot fill the gap left by fiscal support.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: we now have the tightest labor market in decades companies everywhere are raising wages and especially for lower incomes
claims.claim: A very tight labor market has shifted bargaining power to workers, raising wages for the lowest incomes and squeezing profit margins.
claims.direction: wage share up, profit margin down

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: we're really unlikely to get another push against corporate bargaining power from things like new globalization we've already globalized every good we could globalize
claims.claim: The globalization tailwind to margins is exhausted, so no new push against labor bargaining power is available.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: every possible political proposal to address inequality in some way says maybe you should raise corporate taxes they're the lowest they've been in decades
claims.claim: Corporate taxes and antitrust regulation are at multi-decade lows, so political pressure on inequality points toward higher taxes and tougher regulation, a profit headwind.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: there are particular areas like fuel and oil and gas and food that are specifically inelastic and specifically have inflation
claims.claim: Inflation concentrated in inelastic items such as fuel and food squeezes the budgets of the bottom 40-60% of consumers, so non-commodity firms cannot raise prices.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: back then about 30 of the stock market was commodity producers today it's more like 3
claims.claim: In the 1970s about 30% of the stock market was commodity producers who benefited from inflation, now only about 3%, so equities benefit far less from commodity inflation today.
claims.indicator: commodity producer weight in equity index
claims.direction: index profits benefit less from inflation

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: today we're telling companies well maybe you want to spend actually for the resilience of your supply chain
claims.claim: Spending on supply-chain resilience and decarbonization is low-return capex, so it will not lift profits like past investment.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: if interest rates rose one and a half percent on a 10-year bond and maybe you have a 10-year stream of earnings that's a 15 equity decline
claims.claim: Back-of-envelope duration: a 1.5 point rise in the 10-year yield on a 10-year earnings stream implies about a 15% equity decline.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: equities have basically fallen in line with the fact that rates have risen that's it that's all that happens
claims.claim: Equities have only repriced for higher rates, not for lower profits, so no earnings slowdown is priced in.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the market is not expecting a very significant slowdown or a very significant change in the path of earnings for companies
claims.claim: The market embeds a goldilocks scenario of little slowdown, so a profit decline is a downside risk to equities.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: people demanded a higher risk free to be in stocks in an inflationary environment it was harder to control all that
claims.claim: High inflation makes the economy more volatile and raises the required return on stocks, which hurt equities in the 1970s even though profits held up.
claims.direction: equity valuations down when inflation high
claims.testable: yes - inflation regimes vs equity multiples

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: u.s companies are expected to continue doing better than any other companies in the rest of the world
claims.claim: Priced-in US outperformance requires still higher profitability or more market share, and prior decades of single-country success rarely repeat.
